## The player's screen

**The player's screen** (decided 14 November 2026, build order item 18b; the owner: "Yes. But the bigger problem is the ui in amarna right now. It is a mess. No way you can play a game this complex when you can't even tell what is going on on the screen.", then "Agreed, expertly! I think civ 5-6 solved it best for a game like ours, where it shows what hasn't received an order maybe? Yet we are a fusion of civ's turn-based, and paradoxes' real-time. So you don't give constant orders here like in civ, I imagine. So we must have our own system of sorts that fits this game. But looking at civ and paradox does it, and adapting a fusion of it for ours, which also accounts for delay and that we simply just often fully know the state, must be the goal? What is your take, expert?"). A person playing a seat sees at a glance what happened to them, what waits for their answer, what they can do and whether they are winning; everything else is one tap away and never in the way.

As played on 14 November 2026, the orders tab was one scroll about 15,000 pixels tall on a desktop, with 63 drop-downs, about 200 buttons and 100 fields, and the button that ends the season at its foot; the season and inbox tabs listed every move in the world; nine tabs ran off the panel. This document planned the screens of watching and none of playing, so each item added its form to the orders; this section is the missing plan. It takes from Civilization V and VI their turn and from Paradox's games their running clock, as the game already does (orders sealed each season, standing orders carrying on between), and adds what neither has, time and distance. It changes no rule.

**A model seat reads the same** (the owner, 14 November 2026: "These rules about playability must all equally apply to what a model seat sees in any game. All players must play on as equal terms when it comes to readability of the game, as possible. Agreed, expert?"). A model's request is its screen: it carries the same season brief, the same list of what waits for its answer, the same in-flight list and the same ages, and only the actions that apply to what it holds, in the same order as the screen. Both are drawn from one source in the code, the screen's and the request's, so they cannot drift apart, and a test fails where a seat's screen and its request differ in what they say; each part below changes the request in the same pull request as the screen. A change to a request starts a new version ("Same seed, same game"), and is tried with script stand-ins and the free local model, never paid models ("No model games with paid models" in the rules for the builder).

- **Four questions, in order.** The screen answers them top to bottom, each in a line or two before any detail:
  1. **What happened to me?** A season brief of at most six lines, most urgent first: a foreign army in the seat's land or at its border, a battle of its own, a letter or envoy waiting, a promise kept or broken, an errand done, gold or grain running short. Each line jumps to its place on the map and opens what answers it; the world's other moves stay in the season's record.
  2. **What waits for my answer?** Audiences, letters, and servants home with no errand, counted on one button; never a tab that appears and pushes the others aside.
  3. **What can I do?** The actions on the thing selected (below).
  4. **Am I winning?** One line at the top: the seat's place on the scoreboard as its own court can reckon it, with how sure and how old that reckoning is, never the true standing a king could not know.
- **The seal button knows what waits**, as Civilization's end-turn button names the next unit wanting orders. Here nothing needs an order, since standing orders carry everything on, so it counts only what is new or finished since the last seal: a unit that reached where it was sent or whose order ran out, an envoy or servant home without an errand, an audience or letter waiting, a foreign army newly in sight of the seat's land. A tap goes to the next; the season can be sealed at any time, the count beside it.
- **Orders live on the thing**, as in Civilization's unit panel. Select one of the seat's armies or fleets: move, hold, support, its standing order, command at a distance. Select a foreign court on the map: write, send an envoy, give, set a spy. Select one of the seat's provinces: tax, build, raise or dismiss troops, its governor. The court and the treasury (servants and their fees, trade, the archive) have a button each. Only what applies to the selected thing now is shown, as a request shows a model only what applies ("Requests are rules too"): a grant of command only for an army beyond reach of court, a forgery only where a scribe could make one. The council's advice sits on each as a suggestion taken with one tap, its four voices shown where they disagree. The long orders tab goes.
- **What wakes the seat is the player's to set**, as Paradox's alerts and its choice of what pauses the game. An alert bar along the top shows threats and chances, each with its own icon as well as its colour (the core's "Readable by every player"), a tap going to it. "Sleep until something concerns me" becomes that setting: which events wake the seat (a foreign army in its land, an envoy arriving, a letter, a battle, a promise falling due), with sensible defaults and the choice kept.
- **In flight.** One list of everything the seat has set moving and when it lands, by name and season: an envoy to Hatti arriving in Shemu, his answer back by the next Akhet; the seat's word to the army at Ṣumur, arriving next season; Babylonia's twenty shekels, due in Peret; a spy's report. In Civilization and Paradox's games an order lands at once; here a letter takes seasons, so this list is the player's memory, the first thing a person loses track of.
- **Every fact wears its age.** What the seat learned long ago is drawn and written as old: a rival army faint where it was last seen, "seen two seasons ago"; a rival's treasury as a guess with its range, "10 to 20 minas, guessed"; a count of people with the season it was taken. The screen never looks surer than the king is (the core's "No rule untaught"; the "what you know" view under "The main map and its views").
- **The map does the showing.** The seat's own units bright and the rest muted, the season's moves as arrows, threats near its land marked, envoys and letters on their roads; the views and the zoom of "The main map and its views" stay.
- **A top bar, as Paradox's.** Treasury, grain and troops with their change each season, each opening its breakdown, in place of the paragraph of minas and shekels.
- **Records, one tap away.** People, provinces, search, standings, events, the rulebook and the archive go behind one button, whole for those who dig; the old tablets leave the orders, and the graphs of item 18a open there.
- **Watching a seat** shows its brief, its in-flight list and its alerts as it saw them, read-only; god view keeps its own screen ("Spectator mode and analysis").
- **On a phone too:** the same questions and actions at 390 pixels wide, the map above, the brief and the actions in a sheet below it.
- **The first game.** A setup for an evening, where the screen is built and tried first, offered first on the start screen: Egypt, Hatti and Mitanni with the city-states and chiefs between them on that part of the map, the other powers absent, and the random ending drawn on a short curve, with every rule as in the full game (the core's "Different data, same rules"). The player takes any of its seats. First guesses for the balance pass: a median about 20 seasons, a cap near 30.
- **Built in parts, each merged playable**, with pictures before and after: the first game and the season brief; the seal button that knows what waits; orders on the thing; in flight and the ages; the alerts and what wakes the seat; the top bar; Records; the phone. A test plays the first game from the start screen to its end through the screen alone, and fails where the seal button needs scrolling to reach, or where a fact from a past season is shown without its age. Done when a person can play the first game through in an evening, and the full game in a few, telling at each season what is going on.
